title: Contrasting whole-plant hydraulic strategies between light-demanding and shade-tolerant tropical–subtropical ferns
content:
Abstract
Background and Aims
Ferns are one of the most diverse lineages of vascular plants, distributed widely in various habitats of tropical and subtropical forests. Previous studies have indicated that ferns tend to operate conservative stomatal behaviour. However, it is difficult for this finding to explain the abundant fern species in open sites. This study aimed to clarify the whole-plant hydraulic strategy of tropical–subtropical ferns with different light requirements.
Methods
We selected a total of 26 terrestrial fern species (14 light-demanding species and 12 shade-tolerant species) from the tropical–subtropical forests and measured their root [specific root length (SRL)], stem [rhizome; rhizome biomass fraction (RHMF)] and leaf hydraulic (pinna; hydraulic efficiency, drought tolerance, minimum leaf water potential and safety margin) traits. In addition, we compiled a dataset of leaf hydraulic traits for woody and herbaceous angiosperm species from the literature. We analysed the differences in safety margin between ferns and angiosperms, the root–stem–leaf trait relationships and the contrasting whole-plant hydraulic strategies between light-demanding and shade-tolerant fern species.
Key Results
On average, ferns had a more negative stomatal safety margin than woody and herbaceous angiosperm species. In addition, ferns showed a lower leaf hydraulic safety margin than woody angiosperms. Below-ground traits significantly influenced leaf hydraulic safety in ferns; that is, species with lower SRL and higher RHMF showed a higher water potential and leaf hydraulic safety margin. In comparison to fern species from shaded understorey, light-demanding species were associated with higher SRL, lower RHMF and higher leaf hydraulic risk.
Conclusions
We conclude that tropical–subtropical ferns do not exhibit conservative leaf-level hydraulics but rely on a whole-plant strategy involving root acquisition and rhizome storage, which underlies their contrasting performance across light and water availability. This integrative view is crucial for predicting fern responses to habitat disturbance and climate change.
